title: Contingency and sufficient reason
note: The Leibnizian argument asks why there is anything contingent at all. Given the principle of sufficient reason, the whole collection of contingent things needs an explanation, which no contingent thing can supply; so a necessary being exists. Unlike the kalam, it allows the universe to be infinitely old. The main battles are over the principle itself and over explaining wholes.

read.title: Why anything at all?
text: Leibniz held that nothing is so without a reason why it is so. Applied to the world, this principle of sufficient reason yields an argument that does not care how old the universe is:

(1) Every contingent thing has an explanation of its existence. (2) The universe, the sum of all contingent things, is itself contingent. (3) So the universe has an explanation. (4) That explanation cannot be a contingent thing, since every contingent thing is part of what is being explained. (5) So the universe is explained by a necessary being, one that cannot fail to exist.

In Part IX of Hume's Dialogues, Cleanthes objects that this demands too much. If I show you the cause of each of twenty particles of matter, it would be unreasonable to ask further for the cause of the twenty. Paul Edwards later made the same point with five Eskimos on a New York street: explain why each is there, and you have explained why the group is there. This is the Hume-Edwards objection.

Defenders reply that the analogy breaks down when the explanations run only inside the collection. Each Eskimo's presence is explained by things outside the group. But if every contingent thing is explained only by another contingent thing, we still have no answer to why there are any contingent things at all, rather than none. William Rowe and Alexander Pruss press this point. As an image: an endless chain of people borrowing from one another explains no loan unless someone actually has the money.
